    Three steel bridges of the rebuilt city

    An arch, a ladder and a chain bridge, built after the fire of 1923 and lit after dark.

    The Wednesday evening walk. Three steel bridges of the 1920s on one kilometre of river, all lit after dark, then a quick dinner near home and back by about 20:50. Below the timetable are cards to read or hear on the train and at each stop; below those, the history of each bridge. The old-map buttons above show the river before and after the bridges were built: try 1896–1909, then 1927–39.

    A quick dinner near home

    First choice: Kamo to Negi らーめん 鴨to葱, duck ramen. A counter of eleven seats, two or three minutes from Okachimachi station. The broth is made from duck and leeks only. Open 10:00 to 22:30, or until the soup runs out. A bowl is about ¥1,080. Cash only, no bookings, and there is usually a queue. from restaurant listings

    Second choice: Tonkatsu Yamabe とんかつ山家, Okachimachi branch. Pork cutlet with rice and soup for about ¥900 to ¥1,000, eaten at a counter. Its evening hours were not found. hours not found

    Chosen for one person eating quickly: cooked meat, Japanese, a counter, no long sitting. Hōraiya, the old fillet-cutlet house nearby, is shut on Wednesdays; it is on the Thursday page.

    For a day with company: Tamahide 玉ひで in Ningyōchō, founded in 1760, invented oyakodon, chicken and egg on rice, in about 1887. The oyakodon is served at lunch only, 11:30 to 13:30, with a queue. Dinner there is a long sitting of gamecock dishes. from listings and a magazine article

You could see Kiyosu first, walk south to Eitai, and ride the Ōedo line home from Monzen-Nakachō, 12 minutes. The plan above is still better: walking north, Kiyosu Bridge stays in front of you.

    18:10, on the train out

    The line you are riding: the Hibiya line

    Where On the train from Naka-Okachimachi to Kayabachō. The ride is seven minutes; the card takes about five.

    about 4 min to hear

    This is the Hibiya line. Tokyo Metro marks it with the letter H, and its colour on the map is silver. It runs about twenty kilometres, from Kita-Senju in the north-east to Naka-Meguro in the south-west. On the way it touches Ueno, Akihabara, Ginza, Hibiya, Kasumigaseki and Roppongi. Most of it runs under existing streets, which is why it has so many tight curves.

    The line was built to take pressure off the Ginza line, Tokyo's first subway. By the late 1950s the Ginza line was packed. Its platforms could take only six-car trains, already running every two minutes. The planners had a second aim. A private railway, the Tōkyū Tōyoko line, brought commuters from the south-west and stopped at Shibuya. The new line would give those commuters another way into the centre. That is why it ends at Naka-Meguro, beside the Tōyoko line.

    Building began at the north end, where the national railways handed over land for a depot. The first section opened on the twenty-eighth of March 1961. It ran from Minami-Senju to Naka-Okachimachi, the station where you boarded. More sections opened in 1962 and 1963. Then Tokyo was awarded the 1964 Olympic Games, and the finish was brought forward. The last link, from Higashi-Ginza to Kasumigaseki, opened on the twenty-ninth of August 1964, weeks before the Games.

    Who built it? A public body called the Teito Rapid Transit Authority, known as Eidan. The government created it in 1941, in wartime, to run all of Tokyo's subways. It took over two private companies. The first had been started by a businessman, Hayakawa Tokujirō. He opened the first subway in Japan in 1927, between Asakusa and Ueno. The second company ran from Shimbashi to Shibuya. The two were joined end to end in 1939, and together they are today's Ginza line.

    In 2004 Eidan became a company, Tokyo Metro, owned by the national government and the Tokyo government. In October 2024 its shares were listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. The two governments still hold about half.

    Tokyo has a second subway operator, called Toei. It belongs to the Tokyo government alone. After the war Eidan could not build fast enough, so the city was allowed to build lines of its own. Its first line opened in 1960. The two systems were never merged, which is why some changes of train in Tokyo cost a second fare.

    The Hibiya line is one piece of a longer commute. At the north end its trains run straight on to the Tōbu railway, which serves the suburbs north of Tokyo. That through service began in 1962. A second through service, onto the Tōyoko line towards Yokohama, ran from 1964 until 2013.

    About nine hundred thousand people ride the line each day. On its busiest stretch, in the north, trains were measured in 2025 at one hundred and sixty-three per cent of their planned load. That was the highest figure on any Tokyo Metro line. The trains you are riding came into service in 2017. They have seven cars, each twenty metres long, and they replaced shorter cars that had run since the 1960s.

    Two dark events belong to this line. On the twentieth of March 1995 members of a religious cult released the nerve gas sarin on Tokyo subway trains in the morning rush. The Hibiya line was the worst hit, and it was closed for the day. Kodemmachō, which you pass tonight, had more victims than any other station. Then on the eighth of March 2000 a Hibiya line train derailed near Naka-Meguro, and five people died.

    The newest station on the line is Toranomon Hills, which opened in June 2020. It was the first station added to the line in fifty-six years.

    Checked against the Japanese Wikipedia articles on the Hibiya line, Eidan and Tokyo Metro (read 13 November 2026): the opening dates, the Olympic deadline, 1941, 2004, the 2024 listing, the through services, the ridership and crowding figures, the train type, the 1995 and 2000 dates and the five deaths. The reason Tokyo has two operators comes from press commentary seen in summary only. That the 1995 attack was the work of a cult, and that the two early companies became the Ginza line, are from general knowledge.

    18:10, on the train out

    What you are passing: four stations

    Where On the same ride. The stations come in this order: Akihabara, Kodemmachō, Ningyōchō, then Kayabachō, where you get off.

    about 2 min to hear

    Four stations lie between you and the river. Each stands on a piece of old Edo, the city that became Tokyo.

    Akihabara

    Akihabara is named for a shrine, the Akiba shrine, which once stood in an open field here. The shrine was moved in 1890, when a railway company built a freight yard on the site. For decades goods came in here by rail and by canal. Passenger trains began to stop in 1925. After the war, dealers in radio parts set up under the railway arches. In 1949 the American occupation ordered street stalls cleared, and the radio dealers were gathered into small stands there. That is the root of today's electronics district.

    Kodemmachō

    Here stood the main prison of Edo. It held three to four hundred prisoners at a time. It came to this site around 1600 and was closed in 1875. Yoshida Shōin, a young teacher whose pupils went on to lead the Meiji government, was beheaded here in 1859. Today this is an office district with many cloth wholesalers. On the twentieth of March 1995 this station had more victims of the sarin attack than any other. Four people died here.

    Ningyōchō

    The name means doll town. Puppet makers and puppeteers lived here, and puppet theatres and kabuki theatres stood close by. Before 1657 this was also the site of the licensed pleasure quarter of Edo, the Yoshiwara. A great fire destroyed much of the city in 1657. The shogunate then moved the quarter out to fields behind the temple at Asakusa. You come back to this station on foot later tonight.

    Kayabachō

    Kayabachō takes its name from kaya, the reed used for thatched roofs. Thatch dealers lived here in the first years of Edo. Next door is Kabutochō, where the Tokyo Stock Exchange opened in 1878, and many brokers still have offices in these streets. In November 1887 the Tokyo Electric Light Company started a power station here. It sold electricity to nearby customers such as a shipping line and a bank. It is described as the first public electricity supply in Japan. This is your stop.

    From the Japanese Wikipedia articles on each station and district (read 13 November 2026). The power station of 1887 is from the Tokyo Electric Power archive, seen in summary. Sources give 1859 for Yoshida Shōin's death; one Wikipedia page says 1857. That his pupils led the Meiji government is from general knowledge.

    On the walk

    The districts you walk through

    How to use Each note matches one of the coloured patches on the map, and you can read it anywhere on the walk.

    about 6 min to hear

    Tonight you cross five old districts of Tokyo. Each one earned its living in a different way. Together they show how the merchant city of Edo became the money city of modern Japan.

    Each note says what the district was in the Edo period, what changed after 1868, and what you can still see.

    Shinkawa

    Shinkawa is the northern half of an old island called Reiganjima. The island began as a sandbar at the river mouth. A temple, Reigan-ji, was built on it in 1624 and gave the island its name. The great fire of 1657 burned the island, and the temple moved across the river. In 1660 a canal was cut through the island. Its name, Shinkawa, means new canal. Sake wholesalers lined its banks for nearly three hundred years. In the Meiji period the island lost its place as a port. In 1892 a new island, Tsukishima, was built further out in the bay, and ships stopped there instead. The canal was filled in 1948 with rubble from the air raids. Today the island is offices and flats. A few food and drink companies still have offices along the line of the old canal.

    Kabutochō

    Kabutochō means helmet town. A legend says a warrior buried his helmet here, under a mound. A small shrine, the Kabuto shrine, keeps the story. In the Edo period this was marsh, filled in and covered with the houses of great lords. After 1868 it became the money district of Tokyo. In June 1873 the First National Bank opened here. Despite its name it was a private bank. It was chartered under a national banking law. Most of its money came from two merchant houses, Mitsui and Ono. Its manager was Shibusawa Eiichi, a former official. When the Ono house failed in 1875, he became the head of the bank. On the fifteenth of May 1878 the Tokyo stock exchange was founded here. The district burned in 1923 and was rebuilt. After the war the exchange was founded again in April 1949. Trading began on the sixteenth of May. The exchange still stands here. Many brokers have since moved to Marunouchi, and old bank buildings now hold restaurants and a hotel.

    Kakigarachō and Hakozaki

    Kakigarachō means oyster-shell town. The ward says the origin is not certain. The shore here was once a beach of oyster shells, where fishermen dried their nets. In the Edo period it held wholesalers of soy sauce and pottery. A rice exchange opened here in 1876. With the Dōjima exchange in Osaka, it set the price of rice for Japan. In 1872 a shrine called Suitengū moved here. A lord from Kyushu had founded it at his Edo house in 1818. People still come to pray for a safe birth. Its new building opened in 2016. Hakozaki, on the riverside, was the shogun's boat yard and the merchants' warehouse shore. The Mitsui family bought warehouses here in 1740. The Bank of Japan began here in 1882. Then in 1971 an expressway was built over a filled canal. In 1972 a city air terminal opened under the junction. Until 2001 passengers checked in there for flights from Narita. Today it is a bus terminal for the airports.

    Saga and Kiyosumi

    Saga and Kiyosumi lie on the far bank, in the old district of Fukagawa. Saga is said to be named after a port in Kyushu that the shore resembled. In the Edo period it landed dried sardines, sold as fertiliser. Later its grain dealers made it the centre of the grain trade of Tokyo. Kiyosumi was the riverside estate of a lord. In 1878 Iwasaki Yatarō, the founder of Mitsubishi, bought about ten hectares of it. His family made a garden there. In 1923 the garden saved people from the fires. The family gave about half of it to the city in 1924. It opened as Kiyosumi Garden in 1932. Nearby stood a government cement works. In 1883 it was lent to a businessman, Asano Sōichirō. He bought it the next year, with money from Shibusawa Eiichi. Clay from the river bottom and boats for shipping made the site work. Further east were the timber yards of Kiba, there from 1701. They moved out to new land in the bay after 1969. In 2015 an American coffee company opened its first cafe outside the United States here, in an old warehouse.

    Okachimachi

    Okachimachi was named for the okachi, foot guards of the shogun. A map of 1644 already shows their barracks here. A lord from the far north, the lord of Akita, also had a house in the district. In the late Meiji period it became a place of cheap amusement. There were storytelling halls, sideshows and food stalls. The air raids of 1945 burned it out. A black market grew up beside the railway. On the thirtieth of May 1946 about five hundred police raided it. A businessman then built an orderly market of eighty shops. That market grew into Ameyoko. It now has about four hundred shops along five hundred metres of the railway. East of the station is a second trade, jewellery. One recent book counts about two thousand jewellery shops, wholesalers and makers there. In 1964 the name Okachimachi was dropped from official addresses. It lives on in the names of the stations.

    Checked (read 14 November 2026): Shinkawa from Japanese Wikipedia; Kabutochō from Japanese Wikipedia, the First National Bank's company history and a bank's town archive, and the Japan Exchange Group timeline (seen in summary); the meaning of Kakigarachō from Chūō ward's place-name page; Suitengū, the rice exchange, Hakozaki, Saga, Kiyosumi Garden, Okachimachi and Ameyoko from Japanese Wikipedia; the air terminal from English Wikipedia and a news report; the cement works from the cement company's history and the town archive (seen in summary); Kiba from Kōtō ward; the coffee company from architecture press. Not confirmed: Japanese Wikipedia gives 1871 for the First National Bank, but the company history gives June 1873, which is used here. That Kawamura Zuiken dug the canal is tradition only, so it is left out here. The year the timber yards moved to Shin-Kiba is given as 1976 by one source only. The count of two thousand jewellery firms comes from one book. How the jewellery trade began here was not found.

    18:20, walking to the river

    Kayabachō and Shinkawa: money, power and sake

    Where to stand On Reigan Bridge, where Eitai-dōri crosses a narrow canal about 250 metres east of the station, three minutes' walk. Stop at the middle of the bridge on the right-hand footway. Or listen as you walk.

    about 2 min to hear

    You are standing on Reigan Bridge. The narrow water below you is the Kameijima River. Behind you is Kayabachō. In front of you is an old island called Reiganjima. Its northern half was called Shinkawa, which means new canal.

    Think first about what lies behind you. A few streets to the west is Kabutochō. The first modern bank in Japan opened there in 1873, and the Tokyo Stock Exchange in 1878. Close to the station, in November 1887, the Tokyo Electric Light Company started a generating station. From it ran the first public supply of electricity in Japan, to offices nearby. A stone marks the place, a little north of the station crossing.

    Now look ahead, along the street towards the river. In the Edo period this island was the sake quarter of the city. The best sake came by sea from the Kansai, the region around Osaka and Kyoto. People in Edo called it kudari-zake, sake sent down from the capital.

    Cargo ships brought the casks into the bay. Small boats carried them up a canal that cut through this island, to the storehouses of the wholesalers. In 1703 Edo had a hundred and twenty-six sake wholesalers. In time they gathered here, along that canal.

    Tradition says the canal was dug in 1660 by a merchant named Kawamura Zuiken. He was a contractor who grew rich after the great fire of 1657. In 1670 and 1672 he opened the two coastal shipping routes that carried rice to Edo and Osaka from the north of Japan. His house stood on this street, and a signboard near this crossing marks it.

    The canal was about six hundred metres long. It was filled in in 1948. Nothing of the storehouses is left. One thing does survive. Just south of this street, between office blocks, is a small shrine, Shinkawa Daijingū. It burned in the air raids of March 1945. The sake wholesalers rebuilt it in 1952.

    Walk on east. The lit arch of Eitai Bridge will rise ahead of you.

    The canal, Kawamura Zuiken and the sake quarter are from a transcription of Chūō ward's guide to its monuments; the power station is from the Tokyo Electric Power museum page; the shrine is from Japanese Wikipedia; the count of wholesalers is from a sake museum page (read 13 November 2026). Reigan Bridge's position is from OpenStreetMap. Which corner the Zuiken signboard stands on, and whether it is lit, were not found. The 1873 bank and the 1878 exchange are from general knowledge.

    18:32, at Eitai Bridge

    Eitai Bridge: the mouth of the old harbour

    Where to stand On the bridge, on the right-hand footway as you walk out from the west end. That is the downstream side. Stop where the arch is highest beside you, and face the railing.

    about 2 min to hear

    Stand at the top of the arch, on the downstream side, and face the river. The water is flowing away from you, towards the bay.

    Straight ahead the river divides round an island. That is Tsukuda. The lit bridge in front of it is Chūō-ōhashi, finished in 1993. Behind it stand tall apartment towers. They are built on the land of the Ishikawajima shipyard. A Western-style shipyard was opened there in 1853, the year the American warships came. It grew into one of the great shipbuilders of modern Japan. The towers went up after the yard closed.

    You cannot see it, but under the riverbed, about twenty-five metres downstream of you, runs the Tōzai subway line.

    Now think of this river as a road. Until the twentieth century this was the mouth of the city's harbour. Large coastal ships anchored out in the bay. Small boats brought their cargo in past this point, into the canals of the merchant city on your right. Rice, sake, salt, timber and fertiliser all came this way.

    On your left is the Fukagawa bank. Its waterfront was lined with storehouses. The district of Saga there became the centre of the grain trade of Tokyo. In 1897 Shibusawa Eiichi, who founded the first modern bank in Japan, started a warehouse company in Fukagawa. That company still has its head office a short walk from the far end of this bridge.

    On your right, at the west end of the bridge, a small stone stands in the planting. It marks the first school for merchant-ship officers in Japan. The Mitsubishi company opened it in 1875, on a ship moored in the river just below you.

    Now turn round and look upstream, across the road. The first Eitai Bridge, built in 1698, crossed about a hundred metres up that way.

    When you have looked, walk back to the west end and turn right, along the river, to the small white bridge.

    The view of Chūō-ōhashi and the towers is confirmed by night photographs. The subway, the old bridge's position and Saga are from Japanese Wikipedia; the warehouse company is from its own history page; the seamen's-school stone is from the ward monuments guide (read 13 November 2026). The standing spot is an estimate. The shipyard of 1853 and the date of Chūō-ōhashi are from general knowledge. The Skytree may show from the other footway, upstream; that was not confirmed. No marker for the collapse of 1807 was found at the bridge.

    18:52, at Toyomi Bridge

    Toyomi Bridge: where the Bank of Japan began

    Where to stand Cross the small white bridge to its north end. Look for a low stone beside the path, in a small planted space next to the large office block. If you cannot find it, stand at the middle of the bridge.

    about 2 min to hear

    Step off the north end of the white bridge. You are now in Hakozaki. Look for a low stone beside the path. Its inscription reads Nihon Ginkō sōgyō no chi. That means the place where the Bank of Japan began. You may need your phone light to read it.

    In June 1880 the government office that ran the settlement of Hokkaidō opened a sales office here for the products of that northern island. The building was Western in style. Its architect was an Englishman, Josiah Conder, who taught the first generation of Japanese architects.

    That office was abolished in February 1882. The new central bank needed a home. It borrowed this building, and it opened for business here on the tenth of October 1882. It stayed for fourteen years, then moved to its present site, further up this small river. The building burned in the fires of 1923.

    Why here? Because this was the water gate of the merchant city. Turn and look back across the small river, to the south-east. There is the arch of Eitai Bridge, seen from the side.

    The narrow river under the white bridge is the Nihonbashi River. It runs west into the old heart of Edo, past the stock exchange quarter and on to Nihonbashi. Its banks were lined with landing places, each with its storehouses. Boats from the ships in the bay came in here first. In the Edo period an inspection post stood on this corner to check them.

    Now face up the Nihonbashi River, to the west. For a few hundred metres it is open to the sky. After that it runs under an elevated motorway.

    The large office block behind you was the head office of IBM Japan until January 2024.

    Now walk north along the Sumida, towards the next bridge.

    The Bank of Japan stone and its dates are from the Bank's own timeline and a travel site's summary; the inspection post, the storehouses and the motorway are from Japanese Wikipedia; the IBM move is from a news report (read 13 November 2026). The stone's exact position is an estimate, and whether it is lit was not found. Conder as teacher of Japan's first architects is from general knowledge.

    19:00, on the riverside walk

    The far bank: Fukagawa, the warehouse shore

    Where to stand On the riverside path, at or just north of the motorway bridge, about halfway to Kiyosu Bridge. Stop where you can see across the water. If the path is shut, read this at the north end of Toyomi Bridge.

    about 3 min to hear

    You are on the west bank of the Sumida, with the river on your right. Ahead of you, upstream, is Kiyosu Bridge, lit pink. Behind you is the blue arch of Eitai Bridge. Overhead is a motorway bridge, with an ordinary road on its lower level.

    Look across the river. The far bank is Fukagawa. In the Edo period it was the warehouse shore of the city. In the dark you will see apartment blocks and office lights, not storehouses. What is left of the old trade is a set of street markers put up by the ward.

    The blocks straight opposite are called Saga. From the 1600s boats landed dried sardines there. Dried sardines were sold as fertiliser, and that fertiliser fed the cotton and indigo fields of Japan. The ward has marked two landing yards for that trade.

    Rice came to the same shore. A little inland from the bank is the site of the Fukagawa rice market, where dealers traded real rice, sack by sack. Rows of storehouses for rice and oil stood along the water. A canal called the oil canal ran into the river there. It is now buried under an expressway.

    Now look upstream on the far bank, just short of Kiyosu Bridge. There is a gap in the river wall. That is the mouth of the Sendaibori canal. It is named for the storehouse of the Sendai domain, the territory of a great lord in the north, who shipped his rice here.

    Beside that canal mouth, on the nineteenth of May 1875, a government works made the first true cement in Japan. A businessman, Asano Sōichirō, later bought the works. His Asano Cement became one of the great cement firms of modern Japan. A stone marks the place. It is too far away to see from here.

    Last, look at your own bank, ahead and to the left. The land between here and the bridge is Nakasu, which means middle sandbank. Filling of a sandbank in the river began in 1771 and was finished in 1773. Within two years it was a pleasure quarter of restaurants and teahouses. In 1789 the government had it dug away again. The land was filled in a second time in 1886.

    Walk on. Kiyosu Bridge stays in front of you.

    The sites on the far bank are from Kōtō ward's list of historic sites; the Nakasu dates are from Japanese Wikipedia (both read 13 November 2026). A walker reported the west-bank path open end to end in daylight in May 2026; whether it is open and lit at night was not confirmed. The pause point is an estimate from the map. That sardine fertiliser fed cotton and indigo, and why Nakasu was dug away, are from general knowledge.

    19:15, at Kiyosu Bridge

    Kiyosu Bridge: the view from the bank, then from the middle

    Where to stand First, on the riverside path 50 to 80 metres short of the bridge, on the downstream side, looking at the whole span. Then walk up onto the bridge and out to the middle, on the footway on the upstream side.

    about 2 min to hear

    Stand on the riverside path with the bridge in front of you and the river on your right. You are looking upstream, a little east of north. The two pink curves are the chains. The road hangs from them.

    Look above the bridge and to the right. On a clear night a tall lit tower should stand there. That is the Tokyo Skytree, opened in 2012, three and a half kilometres away. From this bank a bridge of the 1920s and a tower of the 2010s line up.

    Now look under the bridge, at its far end. The far bank there is Kiyosumi. Just past the bridge a small river opens to the right. That is the Onagi River. Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the shogunate, had it dug in the 1590s. It brought salt by boat from the salt fields east of the city.

    At the mouth of the Onagi stands a small arched bridge, Mannen Bridge. The artists Hokusai and Hiroshige both drew the bridge that stood there in their day. The present one was opened in 1930. Japanese guidebooks say Kiyosu Bridge looks its best from there. They call it the Cologne view, after the bridge on the Rhine that Kiyosu Bridge copied.

    The poet Bashō lived on the bank just above the Onagi mouth. A small garden marks the site of his hut, with a statue of him facing the river.

    Now walk up onto the bridge and out to the middle. Use the footway on the upstream side.

    Look upstream. The next bridge, about seven hundred metres off, is Shin-Ōhashi. Look down at the far bank and the mouth of the Onagi. Boats bound for the warehouses of Fukagawa and the timber yards beyond came past this point.

    Turn round and look downstream. You can see the motorway bridge you walked under, and the blue arch of Eitai Bridge beyond it. Between them, on the left-hand bank, lay the storehouses of Saga.

    Last, look at the chain beside you. Each link is a flat steel bar. The bars are pinned together end to end. No wire cable is used anywhere on this bridge.

    The view from Mannen Bridge, its date of 1930 and the prints are from Japanese Wikipedia. The Skytree's place behind the bridge is worked out from the map, not from a photograph, so it may sit differently. Both standing spots are estimates. The detour to Mannen Bridge is about 300 metres each way from the east end; it is not in the timetable. The salt canal and Bashō's hut are from general knowledge. Where the bridge's plaques are was not found.

    19:35, walking to the station

    Hamachō and Ningyōchō: playground and marketplace

    Where to stand At the crossing beside the Meijiza theatre, where the narrow street Amazake Yokochō leaves Kiyosubashi-dōri on the left. From the bridge, walk west along Kiyosubashi-dōri to reach it.

    about 2 min to hear

    You are at a crossing beside a large modern theatre, the Meijiza. A theatre of that name has stood in this district since the first years of the Meiji period, in the 1870s.

    The narrow street going off to the west is Amazake Yokochō. Amazake is a sweet drink made from rice. The street is said to be named for a shop that sold it in those same years. Walk down it to reach the station. It is about four hundred metres.

    Behind you, towards the river, is Hamachō Park. In the Edo period it was the riverside estate of a great lord, the Hosokawa of Kumamoto. After the earthquake of 1923 the city made it a park. It opened in 1929, the year after Kiyosu Bridge.

    This district was the playground of Edo. The street ahead leads into Ningyōchō, which means doll town. Puppet theatres stood here, and so did two of the great kabuki houses, the Nakamura-za and the Ichimura-za. In the 1840s the government moved the theatres out to the edge of the city.

    Earlier still, in 1617, the shogunate licensed the first walled pleasure quarter of Edo, the Yoshiwara. It stood a few streets beyond the station. After the great fire of 1657 it was moved to the fields north of Asakusa. The old site is called Moto-Yoshiwara, the original Yoshiwara.

    The district was also a marketplace. A few streets to the south is Kakigarachō. A rice exchange opened there in 1876. In 1883 it became the Tokyo rice exchange. Dealers there did not trade sacks. They traded contracts for rice to be delivered later.

    The exchange was closed in 1939, when the wartime state took control of rice. It reopened in 1952 as a grain exchange. It left the district in 2011 and was wound up in 2013.

    Now walk down Amazake Yokochō. Ningyōchō station is at the far end.

    Hamachō Park, Amazake Yokochō and the Yoshiwara dates are from Japanese Wikipedia; the rice exchange dates are from a bank's town-history page and Wikipedia (read 13 November 2026). The age of the Meijiza and the 1840s removal of the theatres are from general knowledge. No marker was found for the rice exchange or the old Yoshiwara on this route. The standing spot and the walking distance are estimates.

    19:50, on the train back

    Where you get off: Okachimachi

    Where On the train from Ningyōchō to Naka-Okachimachi, a five-minute ride, or on the short walk to dinner.

    about 2 min to hear

    Okachimachi means the town of the okachi. The okachi were low-ranking samurai who guarded the shogun and Edo Castle on foot. They were not allowed to ride. Many of them lived in crowded housing in this district. Their pay was small, so many took side work.

    The railway came in 1925. In that year the raised line through Ueno, Okachimachi and Akihabara to Tokyo Station was opened. Trains have passed overhead ever since, and the space under the tracks became a place to trade.

    After the war that trade became a black market, a market selling goods outside the rationing system. Food was short and the authorities had little control. Stalls spread under and beside the tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi. They sold sweets, then goods from American military stocks, then fish and household goods. The market is still there, and it is called Ameyoko. The name may come from ame, the word for candy, or from America. Both explanations are given.

    A second trade here is jewellery. Many wholesalers of gems and watches work in the streets around the station.

    Near the station stands the Matsuzakaya department store. The firm began in 1611 as a cloth shop in Nagoya. In 1768 it bought a shop here in Ueno and kept that shop's name. The store burned in the earthquake of 1923 and was rebuilt.

    The meaning of the name is from Japanese Wikipedia. The 1925 railway date, the black-market origin of Ameyoko and the Matsuzakaya dates were seen in search summaries of a tourism archive, a Japan Tourism Agency page and the store's history pages, not on the pages themselves. The origin of the jewellery trade was not found.

    Why these bridges were built

    The Great Kantō Earthquake struck on 1 September 1923. Most of the damage in Tokyo came from the fires that followed. Many bridges had steel frames but wooden decks, and the decks burned. People who had run to the river were trapped.

    The government set up a Reconstruction Bureau in February 1924. Its head of civil engineering was Ōta Enzō, and its chief of bridges was Tanaka Yutaka, a railway engineer. The Bureau built over 100 bridges, and Tokyo City built several hundred more. The programme was finished by 1930.

    One architect proposed that every bridge should have the same form. The Bureau refused. Tanaka gave each big Sumida bridge a different structure: an arch at Eitai, a suspension bridge at Kiyosu, a long steel beam at Kototoi. The river became a row of nine different steel bridges, built in about six years.

    On Thursday you see Kachidoki Bridge of 1940, the last of the line. Tonight's bridges are where that programme began.

    The bridges

    1

    Eitai Bridge 永代橋

    Present bridge opened 22 December 1926

    TypeSteel arch in the middle, steel beams at each side. The arch is a tied arch: the road deck ties its two feet together, like the string of a bow, so the arch does not push outward on the soft riverbed.
    Size184.7 m long, 25 m wide
    DesignTanaka Yutaka (outline) and Takenaka Yoshitada (detail), with the architects Yamada Mamoru and Yamaguchi Bunzō advising on its look
    Built byReconstruction Bureau; steel from Kawasaki Shipbuilding, Kobe
    StatusImportant Cultural Property since 2007

    The first bridge, 1698. The shogunate built it to mark the fiftieth birthday of the shogun Tsunayoshi. It was the fourth bridge over the Sumida. It joined the merchant city on the west bank to Fukagawa on the east bank. Fukagawa was the district of timber yards and rice warehouses. Fukagawa trades: not checked

    The collapse of 1807. Crowds going to the festival at Tomioka Hachiman shrine overloaded the wooden bridge and a section fell. More than 1,400 people were killed, injured or missing. It is often called the worst bridge collapse in Japanese history.

    The iron bridge of 1897. A steel truss replaced the wooden bridge, slightly downstream of the old site. It is described as the first iron road bridge in Japan. Trams ran over it from 1904.

    1 September 1923. The 1897 bridge had a steel frame but a wooden deck. In the fires after the earthquake the deck burned. Many people who had fled onto it died by fire or by drowning.

    The bridge of 1926. The Reconstruction Bureau rebuilt it first among the big Sumida bridges. Its form follows the Ludendorff railway bridge over the Rhine at Remagen. It was the first bridge in Japan to span more than 100 metres with a tied arch, and it is the oldest of that type still standing. The foundations were dug inside chambers of compressed air sunk into the riverbed, a method reported as new to Japan.

    The river as a freight road. On one day in 1921, 688 boats passed this point between 07:00 and 17:00. On one day in 2014 the count was 174, over a longer day. The bridge was built high and wide in the middle for that traffic, most of which has gone.

    What to look for. The single blue arch against the towers of Tsukuda. The lines of rivets on the arch ribs, visible from the footpath. The planners called this bridge and Kiyosu Bridge a matched pair: this one heavy and plain, the "gate of the imperial capital".

    2

    Toyomi Bridge 豊海橋

    Present bridge finished September 1927

    TypeA steel frame shaped like a ladder laid on its side, with upright posts and no diagonal braces. Engineers call it a Vierendeel bridge, after its Belgian inventor.
    Size46.1 m long, 8 m wide
    DesignFukuda Takeo, for the Reconstruction Bureau
    Built byYokogawa Bridge Works
    StatusChūō ward cultural property; engineering heritage listing 2022

    Where it stands. It crosses the Nihonbashi River at the point where that river meets the Sumida. The Nihonbashi River was the main canal of the Edo merchant quarter, so this was the water gate of commercial Edo. not checked

    Earlier bridges. Tradition dates the first bridge here to 1698, the same year as Eitai Bridge. The forty-seven rōnin are said to have crossed it in 1703 on their way to Sengaku-ji. An iron bridge of 1903 fell in the 1923 earthquake.

    The bridge of 1927. Work began in May 1926. The ladder form was chosen so that the small bridge would sit well beside the big arch of Eitai Bridge. It keeps its original riveted joints.

    What to look for. The white ladder frame, lit a pale orange. It is short enough to take in whole. Film and television crews use it often. From its north side, look back at the Eitai arch.

    3

    Kiyosu Bridge 清洲橋

    Built March 1925 to March 1928

    TypeSteel suspension bridge. The deck hangs from chains of flat steel bars pinned end to end, not from wire cables. The chains are fixed to the ends of the deck itself and not to blocks in the ground, which suits soft ground.
    Size186.3 m long, 22 m wide
    DesignSuzuki Seiichi, under Tanaka Yutaka; the architects Yamada Mamoru and Yamaguchi Bunzō advised on its look
    Built byReconstruction Bureau, with Japanese engineers only
    StatusImportant Cultural Property since 2007, the first road bridge owned by Tokyo to be listed

    A new crossing. No bridge stood here before 1923. A ferry, the Nakasu ferry, carried people across. The reconstruction plan added a bridge to open a new east–west street.

    The name. It was chosen from suggestions sent in by the public. It joins one character from each bank: Kiyosumi on the east and Nakasu on the west.

    The model. The design follows the suspension bridge over the Rhine at Cologne, then counted among the most beautiful bridges in the world. The Cologne bridge was destroyed in 1945, so this is the surviving example of the form. Cologne bridge's fate: not checked

    New steel. The chains use a high-strength manganese steel, and this was the first bridge to use it. The foundations go down about 30 metres and are faced with granite 50 centimetres thick against salt water.

    The pair. The Bureau planned Kiyosu and Eitai together, one graceful and one heavy. They are the two bridges of the 1920s programme that the state has listed as Important Cultural Properties. Night lighting began in August 2020.

    What to look for. The two curving chains and the pink light. From the bank just downstream, the Tokyo Skytree stands behind the bridge. Skytree view: not checked On the bridge, look at the flat bars and the pins that join them.

    +

    Shin-Ōhashi 新大橋

    Present bridge finished 27 March 1977 · optional stop

    TypeThe deck hangs from straight cables that run from two towers. Engineers call this a cable-stayed bridge.
    Size170 m long, 24 m wide
    Built byTokyo Metropolitan Government; steelwork by IHI
    Why it is hereThis bridge is not from the 1920s. Its predecessor is the reason the 1920s bridges were built in steel.

    The first bridge, 1693. It was the third bridge over the Sumida. The poet Bashō lived nearby and wrote verses on it as it was being built. Hiroshige drew it in his print of people caught in a sudden shower, which Van Gogh later copied in oils.

    The steel bridge of 1912. It opened on 19 July 1912, with a steel frame and stone pillars.

    1 September 1923. It was the only bridge on the Sumida that did not burn. Police and army reservists made people throw their bundles into the river so that the bridge would not catch fire. Thousands crossed it to safety. It became known as the "bridge that saved people".

    After 1977. About 25 metres of the 1912 bridge now stands in the Meiji-mura open-air museum near Nagoya. The memorial to the fire and a stone telling the story of the rescue stand at the west end, beside the police box.

    What to look for. The two memorial stones at the west end, on the Hamachō side. The orange towers of the present bridge. tower colour: not checked

    Not confirmed

    • Whether the riverside path on the west bank is open and lit at night from Toyomi Bridge to Kiyosu Bridge. A walker found it open end to end in daylight in May 2026. The street one block inland is the fallback.
    • The standing spots on the cards were chosen from maps, photographs and walkers' reports, not on the ground. Each card says what was not confirmed.
    • Which exit at Kayabachō is nearest the bridge.
    • The exact time of the last Hibiya line train from Ningyōchō. It is after midnight.
    • The eating places' hours come from listings, not from their own pages. Kamo to Negi may close early when the soup runs out.
    • Walking times and waits for trains are estimates. The two train rides were checked on a Japanese route planner.
    • Toilets: the stations have them; none was confirmed on the riverside path.
    • The places on the map are approximate. The bridge markers sit near mid-span.
    • Each sentence tagged "not checked" comes from general knowledge and was not found in the sources below.
